briefs.sellar-mass:
Brain Tumors in a Child

sellar and suprasellar masses that announce themselves on the growth chart, and posterior fossa masses that announce themselves on the neurologic examinationIs the abnormal finding endocrine or neurologic; for the sella, does the axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and for the posterior fossa, which side and which structure?

DiagnosisPracticeWorkup and management
Bottom line

Ask where the abnormal finding sits. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty with a normal neurologic examination points to the sella; ataxia or crossed findings point to the posterior fossa, where you localize side first and structure second. Image with MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); with papilledema, never tap first.

  • Suprasellar mass: classically a normal neurologic examination (no dysmetria, gait abnormality, focal weakness or skin findings); height crosses downward through percentiles while weight holds, with Tanner 1 past the pubertal gate and papilledema. Growth failure with preserved weight is a hormonal deceleration, not a nutritional one; arrested puberty with it means more than one anterior pituitary axis has failed, and multiple axes point to the stalk, not the gland. Headache and disc edema from obstructive hydrocephalus make the mass midline and suprasellar.
  • Craniopharyngioma: from Rathke pouch remnants; cystic and calcified suprasellar mass on MRI; subtle for years before diagnosis.
  • Posterior fossa mass: 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumors but only 15 to 20% of adult ones, so in a child, ataxia with raised pressure is infratentorial until imaged. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.
  • Hemisphere or vermis: limb dysmetria is hemispheric; a midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared. Both together mean a hemispheric mass large enough to disturb midline structures; ipsilateral facial numbness fits (the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally), and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression.
  • Crossed findings: a cranial nerve palsy on one side and long-tract weakness on the other mean brainstem.
Diagnosis
Localizing signs Cerebellar signs – ipsilateral; the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion; face also ipsilateral; body long tracts contralateral · Hemisphere – limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor · Vermis or midline – truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation · Central nystagmus – direction-changing, gaze-evoked and unsuppressed; peripheral (vertigo) nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation · Raised-pressure headache – daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema · Growth failure – downward crossing of height percentiles after a stable channel, weight preserved; pituitary or hypothalamic causes lose height before weight, nutritional and gastrointestinal causes weight before height ⚠︎ · Pubertal delay – one teaching source gates it at no breast development by age 12 in girls; the threshold conventionally taught is 13 ⚠︎; Tanner 1 at 13 clears either gate, but note which figure you are scored on · Stalk pattern – multiple anterior axes down, with or without posterior failure (diabetes insipidus); stalk compression causes panhypopituitarism, most commonly growth failure from TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) or growth hormone deficiency; morning cortisol, free T4 (thyroxine), TSH and IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) come back low in more than one axis · Gland pattern – a single hypersecreting axis with the others intact
Where is the mass
LocationTumorTell
Suprasellar, midlineCraniopharyngioma: Rathke pouch epithelial remnants in the stalk; the adamantinomatous type peaks at 5 to 14 and 50 to 74 yearsCystic and calcified; growth failure, pubertal delay, bitemporal hemianopsia; years of subtle symptoms
Suprasellar or pineal, midlineGerminoma (can't miss): germ cell tumor; adolescent, often maleDiabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes; non-calcified ⚠︎; beta-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) and AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) usually negative in a pure germinoma, though low beta-hCG can be detected; radiosensitive
IntrasellarProlactinoma or other pituitary adenoma; adolescent or adultNon-calcified; one axis hypersecreting, others intact; galactorrhea and amenorrhea, or acromegalic features
Optic chiasm or nerveOptic pathway glioma (pilocytic astrocytoma); young child, often NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1)Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling; visual loss and afferent pupillary defect precede endocrine failure; may cause diencephalic syndrome (emaciation with a normal appetite)
SellaRathke cleft cyst: same embryologic origin, benign, frequently incidentalNon-enhancing, non-calcified cyst; usually asymptomatic or mild headache
Pituitary stalkLangerhans cell histiocytosis; young childCentral diabetes insipidus with a thickened stalk; lytic skull lesions; seborrheic scalp rash
Cerebellar hemispherePilocytic astrocytoma most classicallyCyst with a mural nodule; ipsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia; falls toward the lesion
Cerebellar vermisMedulloblastoma; early fourth-ventricular obstructionTruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base, limbs relatively spared; typically hyperdense on CT (computed tomography), with restricted diffusion; seeds the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid)
Fourth ventricleEpendymomaTends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle; calcification and cysts common
Middle cerebellar peduncleCarries pontocerebellar inputAtaxia still ipsilateral: a right peduncle gives right-sided signs
PonsDiffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaCrossed findings: cranial nerve palsy one side (diplopia from an abducens palsy is often first), long-tract weakness the other; diffuse pontine expansion

Practice
  1. 14-year-old girl, a year of headaches, now worse height fell from 40th to 3rd percentile over 2 years weight steady at 70th percentile; Tanner 1 Skin, neurologic examination normal; no focal deficit Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · optic disc edema → Cystic, calcified suprasellar mass → height falling while weight holds is endocrine, and Tanner 1 at 14 is a second failed axis, so the stalk is involved; with headache and disc edema the mass is midline and suprasellar, cystic and calcified: craniopharyngioma. A vermian tumor brings truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared, and this examination is clean; subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis, a skin-first diagnosis that does not arrest linear growth
  2. 9-year-old boy, 3 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia gait lists to the left left facial numbness No weakness or sensory loss in the limbs BP 118/72 mm Hg · bilateral papilledema → A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphere → every cerebellar sign is on the left, and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the output decussates twice; limb dysmetria is hemispheric, the face is served ipsilaterally, and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression. The right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side, and a frontal lobe mass gives contralateral weakness
  3. 12-year-old girl, 6 months of morning headaches height crossed from the 75th to the 10th percentile weight steady at the 60th percentile Tanner 1; neurologic examination otherwise normal T 36.8 °C · BP 108/66 mm Hg · papilledema → MRI of the brain with contrast → a height percentile crossing with weight held, arrested puberty and papilledema is a suprasellar mass until imaged: MRI of the brain with contrast, sellar views. A bone age is nonspecific and delays the MRI when papilledema is present
  4. 6-year-old boy, 4 weeks of morning vomiting and unsteadiness truncal and gait ataxia; wide-based stance minimal limb dysmetria MRI: midline vermian mass filling the fourth ventricle, restricted diffusion, no extension through the fourth-ventricular foramina Afebrile · papilledema → Medulloblastoma of the vermis → truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and relatively spared limbs localizes to the vermis; a midline fourth-ventricular mass with restricted diffusion in a child fits medulloblastoma, which seeds drop metastases through the CSF. A cerebellar hemisphere pilocytic astrocytoma gives ipsilateral limb signs and is classically a cyst with a mural nodule; ependymoma tends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle, with calcification and cysts common
  5. 9-year-old boy is seen before planned surgery MRI shows a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass Resection is planned for next week Height has slowed over 2 years; no medications BP 100/64 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery → stalk compression can leave several axes deficient, so measure morning cortisol, free T4 and TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery; secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism are treated before the operation, glucocorticoid first. Growth hormone does not come before the axes that threaten the operation, and a planned resection is not a reason to wait 6 months for another MRI
  6. 5-year-old girl, 4 weeks of worsening double vision progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies right hemiparesis with brisk reflexes MRI: diffuse expansion of the pons Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma → a cranial nerve palsy on one side with long-tract weakness on the other is a crossed finding, which localizes to the brainstem; diffuse expansion of the pons in a child is a diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, and diplopia from an abducens palsy is often its first sign. Medulloblastoma and a cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma give ataxia rather than crossed findings
  7. 14-year-old boy, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg non-calcified suprasellar mass CSF beta-hCG mildly elevated; serum AFP normal Growth and puberty normal so far; no rash or bone pain T 36.9 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Suprasellar germinoma → diabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes, with a non-calcified suprasellar mass, a mildly raised CSF beta-hCG and a normal AFP is a suprasellar germinoma (pure germinomas usually have negative markers, but low levels of beta-hCG can be detected), which is highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy, alone or after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Craniopharyngioma is cystic and calcified, and growth hormone and gonadotropin deficits are often its first endocrine failures; Langerhans cell histiocytosis thickens the stalk and brings lytic skull lesions and a seborrheic scalp rash
  8. 9-year-old boy, 2 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting wide-based gait; right-hand dysmetria bilateral papilledema A lumbar puncture is proposed to measure the pressure T 37.0 °C · BP 116/70 mm Hg → Obtain MRI of the brain instead → papilledema with cerebellar signs means a posterior fossa mass until imaged, and lumbar puncture risks herniation, so image first: MRI of the brain instead. Measuring an opening pressure does not remove that risk, and a noncontrast CT followed by a tap still ends in the tap that papilledema with a posterior fossa mass forbids
  9. 10-year-old girl, 1 day after resection of a suprasellar tumor urine output 350 mL/h serum Na 152 mEq/L urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg Alert and thirsty BP 104/62 mm Hg · HR 112/min → Desmopressin → dilute polyuria with a rising sodium after the stalk has been handled is central diabetes insipidus: desmopressin. Fluid restriction worsens the hypernatremia, and hypertonic saline adds sodium to a patient whose sodium is already high
  10. 12-year-old boy, 2 months of headaches and trouble looking up upgaze palsy convergence-retraction nystagmus light-near dissociation of the pupils No head trauma; visual acuity normal Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · HR 76/min → MRI of the brain, then serum and CSF tumor markers → upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation are Parinaud syndrome, a pineal-region mass; in an adolescent boy that is classically a germinoma, so obtain MRI of the brain first, then serum and CSF tumor markers, the CSF once imaging shows a tap is safe. This is not strabismus, and a noncontrast CT does not characterize the mass or the markers
  11. 8-year-old boy with a newly found suprasellar mass Vomiting and lethargic since this morning Free thyroxine low; cortisol result pending BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · Na 128 mEq/L · glucose 52 mg/dL → Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement → hypotension, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia with a new suprasellar mass is adrenal crisis; give IV hydrocortisone and isotonic saline, and avoid levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement, because thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis
  12. 7-year-old boy with a right cerebellar hemisphere mass on MRI right-hand intention tremor and dysmetria falls toward the right Strength and sensation normal His parents ask why the signs are on the same side as the tumor → Cerebellar output decussates twice → cerebellar output decussates twice, so the two crossings cancel and the signs stay on the same side as the lesion. Cerebellar fibers do cross, and the cerebellum does not control the opposite limbs directly
  13. 15-year-old girl with amenorrhea and galactorrhea Normal growth; Tanner 4 MRI: 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification No headache; visual fields full BP 110/68 mm Hg · prolactin 180 ng/mL · TSH normal · urine pregnancy test negative → Prolactinoma → galactorrhea and amenorrhea with a raised prolactin, a normal TSH and pregnancy test, and a small, non-calcified intrasellar lesion with one axis hypersecreting is a prolactinoma; cabergoline is the preferred dopamine agonist. Craniopharyngioma is a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass, and a Rathke cleft cyst is a non-enhancing, non-calcified cyst that is usually asymptomatic
  14. 9-year-old boy admitted with headache and vomiting MRI: posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus Over the last hour he has become drowsy Pupils equal; no seizure BP 128/70 mm Hg · HR 64/min → Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation → a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and a falling level of consciousness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection. Acetazolamide with outpatient follow-up, or observation, leaves the obstruction untreated
  15. 6-year-old boy with declining vision and nystagmus several café-au-lait macules; axillary freckling thin despite a good appetite Normal stools; no bone pain or fractures Afebrile · HR 96/min · weight below the 5th percentile → MRI of the brain and orbits → café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling point to neurofibromatosis type 1, and declining vision with emaciation despite a good appetite is an optic pathway glioma with diencephalic syndrome: MRI of the brain and orbits. Celiac disease is malabsorption, which costs weight first but brings no visual loss or skin signs, and a skeletal survey looks for bone lesions he does not have
  16. 7-year-old girl with newly confirmed medulloblastoma The tumor was resected 2 weeks ago Recovering well; no back pain Leg strength and bladder function normal Neurologic examination unchanged since discharge Afebrile · no papilledema → MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology → medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging is MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology, the lumbar puncture done at least 10 to 14 days after surgery. Bone marrow and whole-body imaging do not look where it spreads
  17. 11-year-old girl with a known suprasellar mass Vomiting since last night now a depressed level of consciousness CT: dilated lateral and third ventricles BP 132/60 mm Hg · HR 58/min · pupils equal → Neurosurgical CSF diversion → a suprasellar mass that blocks CSF flow at the third ventricle causes obstructive hydrocephalus; a falling level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion. Lumbar puncture risks herniation, and acetazolamide does not relieve an obstruction
  18. 4-year-old boy, 3 weeks of headache headache waking him from sleep morning vomiting Normal neurologic examination; no medications Growth chart normal; no recent head injury Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 92/min → MRI of the brain → headache that wakes him from sleep, with morning vomiting, in a child under six is a red-flag headache: MRI of the brain, because a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor. A diary or migraine prophylaxis delays the diagnosis
  19. 13-year-old girl with a suprasellar mass on MRI loss of both temporal visual fields A year of headaches; height has slowed Visual acuity normal; pupils equal Her parents ask why the outer halves of her vision are missing → Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm → a suprasellar mass presses up on the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibers, which carry the temporal fields, decussate: bitemporal hemianopsia. A lesion behind the chiasm, in the optic tract, gives a homonymous defect (the same hemifield lost in both eyes), and a Meyer loop lesion in the temporal lobe gives contralateral superior quadrantanopia
  20. 10-year-old boy treated 1 year ago with resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma Currently asymptomatic Takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine His parents ask what follow-up he needs BP 102/64 mm Hg · height 25th percentile → Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields → after a craniopharyngioma, surveillance is lifelong and endocrine and visual: serial growth velocity with an annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields. Audiometry does not watch the axes or the visual fields this tumor threatens, and AFP and beta-hCG are germ cell tumor markers
Workup and management
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination focal? If not, the lesion is not hemispheric or in the posterior fossa. Plot the growth chart: height falling with weight holding is endocrine. Count failed axes: growth and puberty together are panhypopituitarism, which localizes to the stalk. Is there posterior pituitary failure? Polyuria makes germinoma or histiocytosis more likely. Is there raised pressure or a field cut? Papilledema or bitemporal hemianopsia makes the mass midline and suprasellar, and the MRI descriptor is calcified and cystic. If the examination is focal, find the side, then the structure.
Management Before surgery – treat secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism before the operation, glucocorticoid before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis in an unrecognized cortisol deficiency. Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone in any new panhypopituitarism. · After surgery – diabetes insipidus can develop in 70% after craniopharyngioma surgery; expect the sodium to rise, not fall, when the stalk has been handled, and treat hypotonic polyuria with desmopressin, not fluid restriction · Obstructive hydrocephalus – a posterior fossa mass with drowsiness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection; a suprasellar mass with a depressed level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion, not lumbar puncture · Germinoma – highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy alone, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by response-based radiation therapy, which has been explored to reduce radiation doses and neurodevelopmental harm · Prolactinoma – cabergoline, the preferred dopamine agonist · After craniopharyngioma – lifelong endocrine and visual surveillance, with surveillance MRI
Papilledema forbids the tap With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first.
Reading a sellar vignette Height crossing down through percentiles with weight steady is endocrine growth failure; it excludes malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease and undernutrition, which cost weight first. Tanner 1 past age 13 is gonadotropin deficiency, a second failed axis, which indicates hypopituitarism rather than short stature alone. Optic disc edema without fever or neck stiffness is raised intracranial pressure without meningitis, from obstructive hydrocephalus at the third ventricle. A normal neurologic examination, including finger-nose-finger testing and gait, excludes the cerebellar compartment and with it medulloblastoma. Normal skin excludes tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas) and neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling), the two phakomatoses whose intracranial lesions are on option lists. No focal deficit and no fever exclude brain abscess, which comes with focal findings and usually fever. A year of headaches before worsening is a slow-growing lesion, not a reassurance; the normal blood pressure and temperature exclude infection and crisis but say nothing about the pituitary; a morning cortisol would.
Pearls Height falling away from a stable weight with Tanner arrest and headache is a suprasellar mass until MRI says otherwise. Plot the growth chart before you order the headache imaging: a height percentile crossing is a localizing sign, and it remains detectable when the neurologic examination is normal. The exception to height-before-weight is the diencephalic syndrome of a hypothalamic glioma: emaciation with a normal appetite. Diabetes insipidus first and anterior axes later makes germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis more likely than craniopharyngioma; send serum beta-hCG and AFP, and CSF levels once imaging shows a tap is safe, before assuming craniopharyngioma. Boundary: untreated acquired primary hypothyroidism reproduces this growth pattern exactly (height arrest, preserved or rising weight, delayed puberty) but does not produce papilledema; check TSH and free T4, and disc edema separates the two. Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six. Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology.
Common wrong answers Subependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles: tuberous sclerosis is a skin-first diagnosis and does not arrest linear growth. Tumor in the cerebellar vermis: truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared; it does not touch the pituitary. Parietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim: abscess is acute, febrile and focal; a year of headaches with growth arrest is not an infection. Enhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal: acoustic neuroma is an adult disease of hearing loss and tinnitus, with no endocrine consequence. Right middle cerebellar peduncle for left-sided signs: the right region on the wrong side. Pineal mass: common in children, but it produces Parinaud syndrome. Germinoma when the anterior axes failed first and there is no polyuria; adenoma when two axes are down, there is no galactorrhea, and CSF flow is blocked; optic glioma with normal skin, normal pupils and weight preserved; Rathke cleft cyst for progressive panhypopituitarism with raised pressure, too much disease for a simple cyst; histiocytosis with normal skin, no polyuria and no bone pain.
Pairs with Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment: the same complaint, a 13-year-old girl with worsening headaches, with the red-flag gate answered in the opposite direction. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern. Headache in a School-Age Child: the workup before localization; is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: posterior fossa tumor as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization. Hyperprolactinemia: the intrasellar adenoma in the adult. Polyuria: the step before this one; is the polyuria water or solute, and is the deprivation test still needed?
Transferable rule

When a mass sits on a midline structure, the localizing finding may be endocrine rather than neurologic: a growth chart and a Tanner stage are examination findings, and in the sellar region they appear years before the field cut and the papilledema. When the finding is neurologic, localize side first and structure second; the cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion.
